title: The sleeping palace
hookLine: he wakes at night to see the musicians asleep and sprawled; the glamour is gone
last: RAHULA — LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.

cards: Two in the morning, the end of a party. The lights come up and the music stops. The room that looked magical an hour ago is just a room: sticky cups, a torn streamer, someone asleep on the couch with their mouth open.

Nothing has changed except the light, and yet everything has. In the story, the prince comes home on the night his son is born, and the palace throws him a celebration: dancers, singers, musicians, all for him.
His mind is somewhere else, and he falls asleep in the middle of it. The performers, seeing no one watching, lie down where they are and sleep too. Sometime in the night, the prince wakes up.

teach.b: The lamps are still burning, and by their light he sees his palace as it really is. The later telling doesn't spare the details. Dancers sprawled across the floor, instruments dropped beside them.
Some snoring, some grinding their teeth, some talking in their sleep, mouths open, clothes in disarray.
The people who dazzled him a few hours ago are just tired bodies now. The great hall, the telling says, looked to him like a burial ground. And earlier that evening, one more thing happened.

A young woman watching him ride by sang a little verse: happy is the mother, happy the father, happy the wife of a man like this. Her word for happy can also mean cooled, at peace, and it's related to nibbana.
The prince heard it and thought: what is it that's truly cooled? And he knew. The fires of wanting, gone out.
Put those two moments together and you have today's teaching. The glamour was never in the palace. It was a spell, a way of seeing, and in one night it broke.
Buddhists call this feeling samvega: a jolt of clear-eyed urgency, the shock of seeing ordinary life plainly.
It isn't disgust with people; the dancers did nothing wrong. It's the moment the prince stops being enchanted and starts being awake to what he'd been looking at all along.

how: Buddhists retell the sleeping palace as the night of the great departure, and teachers point to samvega, the jolt of seeing life plainly, as a healthy spur to practice rather than a reason for gloom.

o: a jolt of urgency from seeing life plainly
a feeling of joy after giving a gift
a deep calm that settles after meditation

games.q: what's inside the night — tap the pairs.
p: happy is the mother, the father

s: the prince was disgusted by the dancers as people
they did nothing wrong. what broke was the spell, the way he'd been seeing.
the young woman's word for happy is related to nibbana
it can mean cooled, at peace, and set him thinking about what is truly cooled.
it's a jolt of urgency and clarity, a spur to wake up.

games.q: you wake in the night and the dazzling hall looks like a room of tired, sprawled bodies. what's happening?
o: the spell has broken: you're seeing it plainly.
games.why: nothing had changed but his seeing. the later telling says the hall looked to him like a burial ground, and that night he decided to leave.

practice: Look around the room you're in as if the lights just came up, and pick one ordinary thing: a chair, a lamp, a pile of laundry, a phone.

See it as if for the first time, its shape, its color, what it's for, what it cost, what it will become when it wears out, not to dislike it, just to see it without the story you usually tell about it.
Then close your eyes and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Samvega. The jolt of clear-eyed urgency the prince felt waking to see his glittering hall by plain lamplight, the spell of it gone.

orig.note: Pali: a stirring, a sense of urgency, the shock of seeing life clearly.

carryVoice: Your line: the spell breaks. The palace didn't change that night; his seeing did. That's day thirty-six.
